title: Adam’s Story and a Warning
setting: Eden, in the shady bower through the afternoon until sunset
summary: Adam asks why the vast heavens should circle the tiny earth; Raphael leaves the question open, sun-centred or earth-centred, and tells him to be ‘lowly wise’. Adam then tells his own story: waking into life, meeting God, naming the animals, asking for a companion, and the creation of Eve. When he confesses that Eve’s beauty overpowers his judgment, Raphael warns him against passion, answers his question about how angels love, and leaves at sunset with a last warning.

sections.title: Adam’s question about the heavens
sections.note: Adam thanks Raphael, then puzzles over a problem: why should huge, noble stars race around the small, motionless earth every day just to give it light?

sections.title: Eve goes to her flowers
sections.note: Seeing Adam turn to abstruse thoughts, Eve slips out to tend her plants. Not because she cannot follow: she would rather hear it later from Adam, who mixes his lessons with caresses.

sections.title: Raphael on astronomers
sections.note: Raphael says the heavens are God’s book to read, but their structure is left to human dispute, perhaps to make God laugh at all the cycles and epicycles. Size and brightness are not worth: the earth may hold more good than the barren sun.

sections.title: What if the sun be center?
sections.note: Raphael floats the new astronomy: the sun at the center, the earth a planet with three motions, perhaps life on the moon and other worlds. Then he closes the question: ‘Heaven is for thee too high… be lowly wise’.

sections.title: Adam offers his own story
sections.note: Adam agrees that the prime wisdom is to know what lies before us in daily life. Eager to keep Raphael longer, he offers to tell his own story.

sections.title: Raphael was away that day
sections.note: Raphael explains that he missed the creation of man: he was guarding the gates of Hell, from which he heard torment and lament.

sections.title: Adam wakes into life
sections.note: Adam remembers waking on a flowery bank, springing up, looking at the sky and naming what he saw, and asking the sun and hills who made him. Falling asleep, he dreams of a divine guide who calls him to the garden.

sections.title: The garden, the command, the names
sections.note: He wakes to find the dream real. God gives him the garden, sternly forbids the one tree, then brings the birds and beasts to be named. Among them Adam does not find what he still wants.

sections.title: Adam asks for a companion
sections.note: In a remarkable dialogue Adam argues with God that there can be no real fellowship between unequals. God teases him (‘what thinkest thou then of me?’) and then reveals it was a test: he already knew it was not good for man to be alone.

sections.title: The creation of Eve
sections.note: Overwhelmed, Adam falls asleep but sees in a trance God take a rib from his side and form a woman. She vanishes; he wakes to seek her, finds her led by God, and cries ‘Bone of my bone, flesh of my flesh’.

sections.title: The nuptial bower
sections.note: Eve turns away, wanting to be wooed; Adam follows, and she yields with ‘obsequious majesty’. The stars, earth, winds and nightingale celebrate their wedding night.

sections.title: Adam confesses Eve’s power
sections.note: Adam admits that nothing else moves him as Eve does: in her presence his higher knowledge seems foolish, and whatever she says seems ‘wisest, virtuousest, discreetest, best’.

sections.title: Raphael’s rebuke
sections.note: Raphael, frowning, tells Adam not to blame Nature but to keep his own judgment: love her, but do not be ruled by her. True love is rooted in reason and leads up to heavenly love.

sections.title: How angels love
sections.note: Half abashed, Adam says it is her grace and their union of minds that delight him, then asks whether angels love. Raphael, blushing ‘celestial rosy red’, says spirits mix wholly, easier than air with air.

sections.title: The parting warning
sections.note: At sunset Raphael leaves with a final charge: stand fast, for standing or falling is in Adam’s own free choice. Adam blesses him and they part.

famous.why: ‘Be lowly wise’: Raphael’s advice to leave the heavens to God and attend to the life in front of you.
Adam’s first words, asking the sun and hills who made him, and feeling ‘that I am happier than I know’.
‘In solitude / What happiness?’: the first human complaint, which God receives as a sign of self-knowledge.
‘Grace was in all her steps, Heaven in her eye, / In every gesture dignity and love’: Adam’s first sight of Eve.
Adam’s confession that Eve seems ‘wisest, virtuousest, discreetest, best’ shows exactly where he is vulnerable.
The angel blushes ‘celestial rosy red, Love’s proper hue’ and describes the love of spirits.

themes: Knowledge has limits: the structure of the heavens matters less than what lies before us in daily life.
Solitude and companionship: Adam argues for a true equal, and God approves his reasoning.
Passion against reason: Adam’s love for Eve is good, but it threatens to overrule his judgment.
Free will again: Raphael’s last words put standing or falling wholly in Adam’s hands.
art: Eve led through the flowering garden toward Adam by an unseen guiding presence, while Adam rises from sleep beneath a tree, his hand stretched toward her.
